questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「シ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「シ」 is shi. 「シ」 has its two short strokes on the left, one above the other, and its long stroke sweeps up from the bottom left. 「ツ」 (tsu) has its short strokes along the top and its long stroke comes down.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「ツ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「ツ」 is tsu. 「ツ」 has two short strokes side by side along the top, and its long stroke comes down from the top right. 「シ」 (shi) has them on the left, with a long stroke that sweeps up.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「ソ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「ソ」 is so. 「ソ」 is one short stroke and one long one, and both come down from the top. 「ン」 (n) looks almost the same, but its long stroke sweeps up from the bottom left.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「ン」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「ン」 is n. In 「ン」 the short stroke sits at the top left and the long stroke sweeps up from the bottom. In 「ソ」 (so) both strokes come down from the top.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「ク」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「ク」 is ku. 「ク」 is two strokes. 「タ」 (ta) is 「ク」 with an extra short stroke inside, and 「ケ」 (ke) has a straight line running out to the right.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「ケ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「ケ」 is ke. 「ケ」 has a horizontal line that runs out to the right with a stroke coming down from its middle. 「ク」 (ku) bends round at the corner instead.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「タ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「タ」 is ta. 「タ」 is 「ク」 (ku) with one more short stroke inside it. That extra stroke is all that separates them.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「ワ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「ワ」 is wa. 「ワ」 has a short vertical line on the left and a hooked top. 「ウ」 (u) adds a short stroke on top, and 「フ」 (fu) has no line on the left.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「ウ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「ウ」 is u. 「ウ」 is 「ワ」 (wa) with a short stroke on top, like the one at the top of hiragana 「う」.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「フ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「フ」 is fu. 「フ」 is a single stroke with no line on the left. Add a vertical on the left and it becomes 「ワ」 (wa); add a short stroke above it and it becomes 「ラ」 (ra).

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「ス」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「ス」 is su. 「ス」 ends with a short stroke kicking out at the bottom right. In 「ヌ」 (nu) the second stroke cuts across the first.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「ヌ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「ヌ」 is nu. In 「ヌ」 the short second stroke crosses the first one. In 「ス」 (su) it kicks out at the bottom right without crossing.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「チ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「チ」 is chi. 「チ」 starts with a short slanting stroke at the top. 「テ」 (te) starts with a flat one, so the top stroke is the thing to check.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「テ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「テ」 is te. 「テ」 has two flat horizontal strokes, then a stroke down to the left. 「チ」 (chi) starts with a slanting stroke instead of a flat one.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「コ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「コ」 is ko. 「コ」 is a box open on the left. 「ロ」 (ro) closes it, 「ユ」 (yu) has a bottom line that runs past the corner, and 「エ」 (e) is shaped like an I.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「ユ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「ユ」 is yu. 「ユ」 has a long bottom line that runs out past the corner. 「コ」 (ko) has two lines of the same length, and 「ヨ」 (yo) has three.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「ロ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「ロ」 is ro. 「ロ」 is a closed box. With its left side missing it would be 「コ」 (ko).

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「マ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「マ」 is ma. 「マ」 has a short stroke at the bottom going down to the right. 「ア」 (a) has a stroke coming down to the left instead.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「ア」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「ア」 is a. 「ア」 has a hooked top with a stroke coming down to the left from its middle. 「マ」 (ma) has a short stroke pointing down to the right.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「ル」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「ル」 is ru. 「ル」 is two strokes, the right one turning up at the end. 「レ」 (re) is only that right-hand stroke.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「ナ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「ナ」 is na. 「ナ」 is a flat horizontal crossed by a stroke that curves down to the left. 「メ」 (me) is two slanting strokes crossing like an x.

questions.stem: Which sound does the katakana 「メ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「メ」 is me. 「メ」 is two slanting strokes crossing like an x. 「ナ」 (na) has a flat horizontal instead.

questions.stem: Which katakana stands for the sound 'shi'?
questions.explanation: shi is written 「シ」. Its short strokes are stacked on the left and the long stroke sweeps up. 「ツ」 is tsu.

questions.stem: Which katakana stands for the sound 'n'?
questions.explanation: n is written 「ン」. Its long stroke sweeps up from the bottom left. 「ソ」, with both strokes coming down, is so.

questions.stem: Which katakana stands for the sound 'tsu'?
questions.explanation: tsu is written 「ツ」. Its short strokes sit side by side along the top and the long stroke comes down. 「シ」 is shi.

questions.stem: Which katakana stands for the sound 'wa'?
questions.explanation: wa is written 「ワ」. It has a short line on the left and no stroke on top. 「ウ」 is u and 「フ」 is fu.

questions.stem: Which katakana stands for the sound 'ku'?
questions.explanation: ku is written 「ク」. It is two strokes with a bend at the corner. 「タ」 (ta) adds a stroke inside, and 「ケ」 (ke) has a straight line running out to the right.

questions.stem: Which katakana stands for the sound 'su'?
questions.explanation: su is written 「ス」. Its second stroke kicks out at the bottom right. In 「ヌ」 (nu) the second stroke crosses the first.

questions.stem: Which katakana stands for the sound 'chi'?
questions.explanation: chi is written 「チ」. It starts with a slanting stroke at the top. 「テ」 (te) starts with a flat one.

questions.stem: Which katakana stands for the sound 'yo'?
questions.explanation: yo is written 「ヨ」. It has three horizontal lines, open on the left. 「ユ」 (yu) has two, with a long bottom line.

questions.stem: What does the 「ー」 in 「ケーキ」 do?
options: It doubles the k that follows
It marks a pause between words
It shows the word is a name
It makes the e sound long
questions.explanation: In katakana a long vowel is shown with the mark ー, so ケーキ is keeki, cake. Hiragana would add a vowel kana instead, as in おかあさん.

questions.stem: How do you read 「コーヒー」?
questions.explanation: Each ー holds the vowel before it for an extra beat: ko-o-hi-i, written koohii in romaji. Dropping either mark changes the length the word is said with.

questions.stem: How do you read 「スーパー」?
questions.explanation: Both vowels are long, so スーパー is suupaa, supermarket. Like many loanwords it is shortened from the English: suupaamaaketto became suupaa.

questions.stem: How is the long-vowel mark 「ー」 written in vertical text?
options: as a small dot beside the kana
questions.explanation: The mark follows the direction of the writing, so in vertical text it becomes a short vertical line. A horizontal bar would cut across the column.

questions.stem: How is a long vowel usually shown in katakana?
options: with a small ッ after the kana
by writing the same kana twice
with the mark ー after the kana
questions.explanation: Katakana uses ー for long vowels, as in ケーキ and コーヒー. A small ッ doubles a consonant instead, and the two short strokes voice a sound.

questions.stem: How do you read 「シャツ」?
questions.explanation: A small 「ャ」 blends with 「シ」 into one beat, sha: シャツ is shatsu, shirt. A full-size 「ヤ」 would give shi-ya.

questions.stem: How do you read 「ジュース」?
questions.explanation: 「ジュ」 is ju, ー lengthens it, and 「ス」 is su: juusu, juice. Without dakuten, 「シュ」 would be shu.

questions.stem: How do you read 「チョコレート」?
questions.explanation: 「チョ」 is cho, and the ー after 「レ」 makes the e long: chokoreeto, chocolate. The ー is easy to skip, but it is a full beat.

questions.stem: How do you read 「ベッド」?
questions.explanation: A small 「ッ」 doubles the consonant after it: beddo, bed. Read as a full 「ツ」 it would be betsudo, which is not a word.

questions.stem: How do you read 「サッカー」?
questions.explanation: The small 「ッ」 doubles the k and ー lengthens the final a: sakkaa, soccer.

questions.stem: How do you read 「キャンプ」?
questions.explanation: 「キャ」 is kya, 「ン」 is n and 「プ」, with its small circle, is pu: kyanpu, camping. Two strokes instead of the circle would give bu.

questions.stem: In 「カップ」, what does the small 「ッ」 do?
options: It doubles the p, with a short pause before it
It adds a separate tsu sound after the a
It turns the p that follows into a b sound
It makes the a in ka into a long vowel
questions.explanation: As in hiragana, a small 「ッ」 is a one-beat pause that doubles the next consonant: kappu, cup. It is never read tsu.

questions.stem: How do you read 「パーティー」?
questions.explanation: 「ティ」 is a katakana-only combination for the English ti sound, so パーティー is paatii, party. Reading it as 「チ」 (chi) gives paachii, which is not the word.

questions.stem: Which sound does 「ディ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「デ」 with a small 「ィ」 is di, as in ディナー (dinner). Plain 「ジ」 is ji, which is the closest sound traditional Japanese has.

questions.stem: Which sound does 「ファ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「フ」 with a small 「ァ」 blends into fa, one beat, as in ファン (fan). A full-size 「ア」 would make it two beats, fu-a.

questions.stem: Which sound does 「フィ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「フ」 with a small 「ィ」 is fi, as in フィジー (Fiji). 「フェ」 would be fe.

questions.stem: Which sound does 「ウィ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「ウ」 with a small 「ィ」 is wi, as in ハロウィン (Halloween). 「ウェ」 would be we.

questions.stem: Which sound does 「ウォ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「ウ」 with a small 「ォ」 is wo, as in ウォーキング (walking). The small kana blends into one beat rather than being read u-o.

questions.stem: Which foreign sound was 「ヴ」 made to write?
questions.explanation: 「ヴ」 is 「ウ」 with dakuten, made for the v sound in words like violin. Many words that have a v in English are still written with the バ row instead, as in テレビ.

questions.stem: Which sound does 「チェ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「チ」 with a small 「ェ」 is che, as in チェス (chess). 「シェ」 is she and 「ジェ」 is je.

questions.stem: Which sound does 「シェ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「シ」 with a small 「ェ」 is she, as in シェフ (chef). Plain 「セ」 is se, and with dakuten, 「ジェ」 is je.

questions.stem: Which sound does 「ジェ」 stand for?
questions.explanation: 「ジ」 with a small 「ェ」 is je, as in ジェット (jet). 「ゼ」 is ze, and without dakuten 「チェ」 is che.

questions.stem: Why do combinations like 「ティ」 and 「ファ」 exist only in katakana?
options: they are older than any of the hiragana characters
hiragana is not allowed to use any small kana
they are used only for Japanese family names
they write foreign sounds traditional Japanese lacked
questions.explanation: Katakana writes loanwords, so it gained extra combinations for sounds like ti, fa and she that native Japanese words never needed. Hiragana does use small kana, as in きゃ and きって.

questions.stem: What does 「シェフ」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「シェ」 is she, so シェフ is shefu, chef. Chess is チェス, jet is ジェット, and shelf would need a ル: シェルフ.

questions.stem: What does 「チェス」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「チェ」 is che, so チェス is chesu, chess. Cheese is チーズ (chiizu), with a long i and dakuten on the last kana.

questions.stem: What does 「コンピューター」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「コンピューター」 is konpyuutaa. The English -er ending becomes a long aa.

questions.stem: What does 「ハンバーガー」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「ハンバーガー」 is hanbaagaa, with both long vowels shown by ー.

questions.stem: What does 「オーストラリア」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「オーストラリア」 is oosutoraria. Austria is オーストリア, one kana shorter, so read to the end.

questions.stem: What does 「メルボルン」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「メルボルン」 is meruborun: l becomes r, and vowels are added after the consonants.

questions.stem: What does 「アイスクリーム」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「アイスクリーム」 is aisukuriimu. Ice skating would end in スケート.

questions.stem: What does 「テレビ」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「テレビ」 is terebi, shortened from terebijon. The English v has become b.

questions.stem: What does 「ジュース」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「ジュース」 is juusu. Jeans is ジーンズ and shoes is シューズ.

questions.stem: What does 「ノート」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「ノート」 is nooto. In Japanese the word means an exercise book or notebook.

questions.stem: What does 「シドニー」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「シドニー」 is shidonii: the s before i is written with 「シ」.

questions.stem: What does 「パン」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「パン」 is pan, borrowed from Portuguese long before English loanwords arrived. A pen is ペン.

questions.stem: What does 「アルバイト」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「アルバイト」 is arubaito, borrowed from the German word for work. A photo album is アルバム.

questions.stem: What does 「ニュージーランド」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「ニュージーランド」 is nyuujiirando. The small 「ュ」 blends 「ニ」 into nyu.

questions.stem: What does 「フランス」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「フランス」 is furansu. Finland is フィンランド and Fiji is フィジー.

questions.stem: What does 「ドイツ」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「ドイツ」 is doitsu. Japanese uses a name for Germany that sounds nothing like the English one, so it has to be learned.

questions.stem: What does 「レストラン」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「レストラン」 is resutoran: vowels are added after the s and the t, and the final t is dropped.

questions.stem: What does 「アメリカ」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「アメリカ」 is amerika. Africa is アフリカ, which differs by one kana.

questions.stem: How do you read 「コンピューター」?
questions.explanation: 「コンピューター」 is konpyuutaa: 「ピュ」 is pyu, and each ー is a long vowel: kon-pyu-u-ta-a.

questions.stem: How do you read 「ハンバーガー」?
questions.explanation: 「ハンバーガー」 is hanbaagaa: both 「バ」 and 「ガ」 are followed by ー, and both have dakuten.

questions.stem: How do you read 「オーストラリア」?
questions.explanation: 「オーストラリア」 is oosutoraria: the ー after 「オ」 makes it oo, and every kana after it is read in turn.

questions.stem: How do you read 「メルボルン」?
questions.explanation: 「メルボルン」 is meruborun: 「ボ」 has dakuten, so it is bo, and the word ends with 「ン」 (n).

questions.stem: Why does English 'milk' become 「ミルク」, with three kana?
options: every katakana loanword has to end with a u sound
most kana are a consonant plus a vowel, so vowels are added
katakana words must always have at least three characters
Japanese speakers add a ku to the end of every loanword
questions.explanation: Apart from ン, a kana cannot stand for a consonant on its own, so m-l-k gets vowels after its consonants: mi-ru-ku. The l also becomes r, because Japanese has one sound covering both.

questions.stem: English l and r are both written with which row of katakana?
questions.explanation: Japanese has a single sound between English l and r, written with the ラ row: ホテル (hoteru) uses it for an l and レストラン (resutoran) for an r.

questions.stem: In 「テレビ」, which sound has the English v become?
questions.explanation: Japanese traditionally has no v, so it is usually written with the バ row: terebi. The katakana ヴ exists for v, but many common words keep the b.

questions.stem: How does katakana usually write the th of 'Smith'?
options: as f, so Smith is スミフ
as z, so Smith is スミズ
as s, so Smith is スミス
as t, so Smith is スミト
questions.explanation: Japanese has no th sound, and the nearest it uses is s: スミス (sumisu), サンキュー (sankyuu) for thank you.

questions.stem: English words ending in -er, like 'computer', usually end in katakana with:
options: a small ッ before the last kana
a long aa sound, written with ー
the katakana ル (ru) on the end
the katakana ン (n) on the end
questions.explanation: The -er ending is heard as a long a: コンピューター (konpyuutaa), ハンバーガー (hanbaagaa). The final r is not sounded in the Japanese form, so no ル is added.

questions.stem: Which of these is normally written in katakana?
options: the ending of a verb such as 〜ます
questions.explanation: Katakana writes loanwords, foreign names and many sound words. Particles and verb endings are hiragana, and やま is a native Japanese word.

questions.stem: What does 「ワンワン」 describe?
questions.explanation: Sound words like ワンワン (wanwan, woof woof) are often written in katakana. A cat says ニャー (nyaa), and a pounding heart goes ドキドキ (dokidoki).

questions.stem: Where did katakana come from?
questions.explanation: Katakana was made by taking a part of a kanji, which is why its shapes are short and angular. Hiragana is the script that grew from cursive forms of whole kanji.

questions.stem: Katakana 「ハ」 comes from which kanji?
questions.explanation: 「ハ」 (ha) comes from 「八」 (eight), and the two still look almost the same. 「人」 is a person and joins at the top, which 「ハ」 does not.

questions.stem: Katakana 「ミ」 comes from which kanji?
questions.explanation: 「ミ」 (mi) comes from 「三」 (three), whose three strokes it keeps, slanted. 「川」 is the source of 「ツ」, and 「二」 of 「ニ」.

questions.stem: A comic writes 「スゴイ！」 instead of 「すごい！」. Why?
options: because exclamations must always be in katakana
because comics are not allowed to use hiragana
for emphasis, a little like bold type in English
because すごい is a word borrowed from English
questions.explanation: Writing a Japanese word in katakana makes it stand out, a little like bold or italics. すごい (great) is a native word normally written in hiragana.

questions.stem: How would an Australian student's name, such as Emily, normally be written in Japanese?
questions.explanation: Foreign names are written in katakana by their sound: エミリー (emirii), with ー for the long i at the end.
